title: How Netanyahu is trying to discredit Arab parties in bid to block Eisenkot
gist: Ben Caspit reports that Netanyahu, whose Likud won 27 seats but whose bloc holds only 53 of 120 Knesset seats, is campaigning to delegitimize Arab parties' record 19-seat breakthrough to block Gadi Eisenkot's 48-seat bloc from forming a government. Record Arab turnout has made Arab parties potential kingmakers.

insights.claim: Netanyahu's Likud came first in the Oct. 27 elections with 27 seats, but his bloc commands just 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, eight short of the 61-seat majority.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: Neither side can govern without new partners, extending Israel's political uncertainty.

insights.claim: Gadi Eisenkot's bloc holds only 48 seats, even further than Netanyahu's from the 61-seat governing threshold.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: An Eisenkot government is only arithmetically viable with Arab party support.

insights.claim: Israel's Arab minority, about 21% of the population, turned out in record numbers and delivered a combined 19 Knesset seats to Arab parties.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: Arab political mobilization reshapes Israeli coalition math for future elections.

insights.claim: The surge in support for Arab parties may be the most consequential outcome of Israel's election because it makes them potential kingmakers.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: Coalition formation now hinges on whether Jewish parties accept Arab partners, a structural shift in Israeli politics.

insights.claim: Netanyahu has launched a campaign to delegitimize the Arab parties' electoral breakthrough in order to prevent Eisenkot from assembling a government.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: Polarizing tactics raise odds of protracted deadlock or a repeat election.

insights.claim: By casting Arab parties' victory as illegitimate, Netanyahu aims to make an Eisenkot coalition dependent on Arab support politically untenable, preserving his position as caretaker.
insights.speaker: Ben Caspit
insights.so_what: A prolonged caretaker period favors policy continuity on security but stalls economic decisions.
